title: Generics

outcomes.can: Write a generic method that returns the caller's own type.
Read the error when the types in one call do not agree.
Use a generic type with different payloads.
Use a constraint to compare values of an unknown type.

intro: A method that returns the first item of a list should work for a list of anything, and give back that same kind of thing. Generics let you write it once. This module covers generic methods, generic types and constraints.

steps.title: A type that the caller chooses
steps.text: T FirstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback) is a generic method. T is a type parameter: a placeholder that each call fills in. Called with a List<int>, T is int, so the fallback must be an int and the result is an int. Called with a List<string>, the same code returns a string. The compiler works T out from the arguments, so you rarely write it yourself. A type can be generic too. record Pair<T>(T First, T Second) holds two values of one type, whichever type the code that uses it picks. List<T> and Dictionary<TKey, TValue> are generic types you have used already.

steps.title: Predict the types
steps.text: FirstOr is called once with ints and once with strings. Predict the three lines of output.

steps.title: Follow each call
steps.text: The first call returns 4, the first item, as an int, so number + 1 is 5. The second list is empty, so the fallback "none" comes back as a string, and its Length is 4. No conversion was needed in either case: the result has the caller's type. pair is a Pair<string>, so Second is a string.

steps.title: Mix two types in one call
steps.text: This call passes a list of ints and a string fallback. Read the example before checking.

steps.title: Read the compiler error
steps.text: Check the example. T has to be one type for the whole call. The list says int and the fallback says string, so the compiler cannot choose and reports CS0411: the type arguments cannot be inferred from the usage. The relationship between the parameters is checked before anything runs.

steps.title: Ask for an ability
steps.text: Inside a generic method you know nothing about T, so you cannot compare two T values with > or call methods on them. A constraint states what T must be able to do. where T : IComparable<T> accepts only types that can be compared with themselves, which includes int and string. Then a.CompareTo(b) is allowed. It returns a number above 0 when a comes after b, 0 when they are equal, and a number below 0 when a comes before b.

steps.title: Return the last item
steps.text: The starter always returns the fallback. Make it work for a list of any type.

steps.title: Carry a result of any type
steps.text: Work from the prompt. The same three methods are checked with numbers and with text.

questions.prompt: What are the three lines of output?

choices.feedback: The first line prints number + 1, and number is 4.
number is 4, so 5 prints. title is "none", which has 4 characters. Second is "Ship".
The second list is empty, so title is the fallback "none", and its Length is 4.

questions.prompt: What happens when you check this example?

choices.feedback: The call does not compile, because T cannot be both int and string.
The list is not empty, and the call does not compile in any case.

choices.text: The compiler reports an error on line 10.
choices.feedback: One call needs one T. A List<int> with a string fallback gives CS0411.

review.evidence: Open a fresh starter on a later visit, with the earlier answer closed. A first unaided pass on every case is later evidence of the skill. A hinted pass stays recorded as assisted.

drillGap: These drills practise one generic declaration each. They do not check one method with several types.
